title: Modeling and estimation of untapped residues from bark content of commercial plantations as a potential source of renewable energy
content:
Abstract
Bark, characterized by high lignocellulose content, low ash variability, and a favorable calorific value, represents a promising yet underutilized feedstock for low-carbon bioenergy production. Short-rotation woody crops (SRWC’s) provide an ideal source for bioenergy production due to their rapid biomass accumulation. While logging residues from these crops are increasingly recovered, the bark fraction remains largely overlooked despite its localized abundance and low marginal cost. This study aimed to: (i) quantify absolute and relative bark thickness and biomass; (ii) develop predictive allometric models linking bark traits to tree-level variables (diameter at breast height (DBH) and total height); and (iii) evaluate the thermochemical fuel properties of bark. A systematic grid sampling design was used to establish 64 plots across 10 SRWC species (six conifers and four broadleaves) in northern Iran. Measurements of DBH, total height, and merchantable height were obtained from 1877 trees, while bark samples were analyzed for calorific value, ash content, fuel value index, and energy content. Bark content accounted for 11%–17% of total stem biomass in broadleaves (4.9–13.5 Mg ha−1) and 11%–25% in coniferous (2.8–6.7 Mg ha−1). Although coniferous exhibited a 24% greater average bark thickness, their total bark biomass yield was 48% lower than that of broadleaves. Bark moisture content peaked in Quercus castaneifolia and Taxodium distichum (>25%) and was lowest in Alnus subcordata and Pinus taeda (<15%). Fuel quality evaluation via ash content revealed that Acer platanoides and Populus deltoides exceeded 4%, whereas T. distichum remained below 2%. Broadleaves yielded 55% more potential energy per ha than coniferous, with P. deltoides and Alnus subcordata exceeding 11 GJ ha−1. Based on the integrated fuel value index, A. subcordata and T. distichum emerged as the most viable species for bioenergy deployment. This study establishes a practical, non-destructive empirical framework for quantifying and modeling bark biomass and thickness, offering critical data to guide species selection for decentralized biomass valorization.
